meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I find television very educating. Every time somebody turns on the set, I go into the other room and read a book'?
meta.ogDescription: Credited to Groucho Marx and documented in 1950 — yet his own written version reads differently. Quote Investigator traces all the variants.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1890–1977 · American comedian, Marx Brothers star, host of You Bet Your Life
answer.sourceLine: Quote Investigator ↗ credits the quip to Groucho and finds this wording in print by August 1950 — bar the comma after “set,” which later printings add — as a freestanding item in Reader’s Digest signed with his name. But the version Groucho demonstrably wrote himself — in his essay “King Leer” for the TV-listings magazine Tele-Views, which ran shortly before his October 1950 television debut and is reported as September 1950 — is worded differently, so the familiar sentence cannot be pinned to anything he is documented to have written.

source.excerpt: I must say I find television very educational. The minute somebody turns it on, I go into the library and read a good book.
trail: August 1950 — The earliest printing found by Quote Investigator ↗ is a freestanding filler item in Reader’s Digest carrying the familiar wording and signed simply “Groucho Marx” — no interview, no source note.
3 August 1950 — The Christian Science Monitor reprints it under the heading “Marx on TV,” crediting Reader’s Digest, as transcribed by QI ↗. Newspaper reprints continue through 1951.

Before October 1950 — Groucho’s own essay “King Leer” appears in the TV-listings magazine Tele-Views, closing by asking readers to watch the television debut of You Bet Your Life that October, with a different wording. The September 1950 month is an assertion by Robert S. Bader’s 1993 collection Groucho Marx and Other Short Stories and Tall Tales, relayed by Quote Investigator ↗, which says it has not identified the precise issue of Tele-Views. The essay is reprinted, undated, in The Essential Groucho (2000) ↗.

25 November 1950 — Bennett Cerf’s Saturday Review column reports that Groucho said the Reader’s Digest wording to Doubleday editor Ken McCormick — the only named route by which that version may have reached print, per QI ↗.
source.excerptNote: This is the wording Groucho wrote, as transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗ — not the sentence that became famous. In the essay he immediately calls the attitude “cynical” and adds that now that he is part of television he doesn’t mean a word of it, before urging readers to watch his new show.

source.rightsNote: Both documented forms of this line were first published in 1950 — the familiar wording in Reader’s Digest in August, Groucho’s own version in Tele-Views shortly before his October debut — well after the pre-1931 cutoff for US public domain by age, so neither can be treated as public domain here. Rights would rest with Groucho Marx’s estate and the original publishers, with the 2000 Essential Groucho reprint separately in copyright to Vintage Books.

author.name: Groucho Marx
author.heading: Who was Groucho Marx?
author.metaLine: 1890–1977 · American comedian, Marx Brothers star, host of You Bet Your Life
author.bio: Born Julius Henry Marx in New York City in 1890, Groucho went from vaudeville with his brothers to thirteen Marx Brothers features, among them Animal Crackers, Duck Soup and A Night at the Opera. He was also a working writer — essays for magazines and books including Groucho and Me (1959) and The Groucho Letters (1967) — which matters here, because the television gag survives in a piece he wrote rather than merely a line someone remembered. In October 1950 he took the quiz show You Bet Your Life onto NBC television, where it ran until 1961.

misattribution.heading: The problem isn’t who — it’s which words
misattribution.intro: Groucho Marx is one of the internet’s great fake-quote magnets, so the usual suspicion applies. Here it lands somewhere unusual: the attribution holds up, and it is the wording that has come loose. At least three sentences circulate as “the” Groucho television quote, and the most famous of them is not the one he is documented to have written.

items.who: “I find television very educating. Every time somebody turns on the set, I go into the other room and read a book.”
items.why: This is the wording that spread — it is essentially what Reader’s Digest printed in August 1950 (that item, as transcribed by QI from the page, carries no comma after “set”) and what Bennett Cerf repeated in Saturday Review that November, reporting that Groucho had said it to Doubleday editor Ken McCormick. But Quote Investigator ↗ notes that the version Groucho wrote himself reads: “I must say I find television very educational. The minute somebody turns it on, I go into the library and read a good book.”

items.who: “…Every time someone switches it on I go into another room and read a good book.”
items.why: A blend of the other two, listed on Wikiquote ↗ among its sourced quotes with a citation to Leslie Halliwell’s Filmgoer’s Companion (1984). Quote Investigator’s reading is that several later renderings like this one are composites of the 1950 wordings.

The Yale Book of Quotations gives 1947 for the essay, a date Garson O’Toole flags as unexplained ↗: the piece closes by asking readers to watch You Bet Your Life, which reached television in October 1950, so it can only have run shortly before that. Nobody has produced the issue — The Essential Groucho (2000) reprints the essay with no date at all, crediting only Tele-Views, and O’Toole was still asking fellow researchers for access to 1950 runs of the magazine.

misattribution.truthLine: Credit the joke to Groucho Marx — Quote Investigator ↗ says so plainly — but know that you are quoting the 1950 magazine wording, not the sentence he set down under his own byline.

context.heading: The joke was an advertisement
lead: The line reads like a swipe at television, and for decades it has been quoted that way — the highbrow comedian refusing the idiot box. The timing says something stranger. In 1950 Groucho was about to become a television star: You Bet Your Life moved onto NBC television that October, and the essay in which he set the gag down in his own words, “King Leer,” was written for a TV-listings magazine to trail that debut.

So the most anti-TV quip in circulation was, in its documented form, promotional copy for a TV show. Groucho knew it, and said so on the spot: having delivered the line, he called the attitude cynical and noted that now he was part of television he didn’t mean a word of it, per Quote Investigator’s transcription of the essay ↗.
detailsBody: A gag delivered in conversation, printed as a magazine filler, rewritten by its author for a listings magazine and then re-quoted by columnists is exactly the kind of text that drifts. “Educating” and “educational” swap places; “the other room” becomes “the library”; “a book” becomes “a good book.”

Quote Investigator allows that Groucho may have used more than one formulation, and finds several later renderings to be composites of the earlier ones — which is why no single sentence can be called the definitive original.
context.pull: The most anti-television joke in circulation was, in its documented form, an ad for a television show.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator investigated this quote, found the earliest citation in Reader's Digest, August 1950 with the popular wording (QI's transcription has no comma after "set") credited to Groucho Marx, documents the Christian Science Monitor reprint of 3 August 1950 headed "Marx on TV", Bennett Cerf's 25 November 1950 Saturday Review column reporting Groucho said it to Ken McCormick of Doubleday, and Groucho's own differently worded version in "King Leer" written for Tele-Views (QI has not identified the precise issue; it relays a September 1950 month asserted by Robert S. Bader's 1993 collection, and notes the essay ran shortly before the October 1950 debut); QI concludes the quip should be credited to Groucho Marx though multiple versions exist, with "King Leer" having the most transparent provenance.

Wikiquote's Groucho Marx page lists the variant "I find television very educational. Every time someone switches it on I go into another room and read a good book" among its sourced quotes, citing Halliwell's Filmgoer's Companion (1984) by Leslie Halliwell.

Garson O'Toole's ADS-L post lays out the conflicting data on this quote, noting the August 1950 Reader's Digest citation, that a September (or August) 1950 date for "King Leer" in Tele-Views "makes sense" given the essay's October 1950 promotional close while asking for help accessing 1950 issues of the magazine, the undated reprint in The Essential Groucho (2000), and the Yale Book of Quotations' unexplained 1947 date for "King Leer".
The Internet Archive hosts a borrowable copy of The Essential Groucho: Writings by, for, and about Groucho Marx, edited by Stefan Kanfer, published by Vintage Books in 2000.

Groucho Marx was born Julius Henry Marx on 2 October 1890 in New York City and died 19 August 1977; he appeared in thirteen Marx Brothers features, wrote books including Groucho and Me (1959) and The Groucho Letters (1967), and hosted the television version of You Bet Your Life on NBC from October 1950 to 1961.
Goodreads reproduces the popular wording credited to Groucho Marx with no source book cited, noting quotes are community-added and unverified — evidence of how the unsourced form circulates.
